correctness.rationale: For \(n=m+1\), the positive unit ball of \(N_m\) has only the nonzero vertices \(e_i\) and \(v=(1/m,\ldots,1/m)\): on a coordinate face it is a simplex, while a full-support vertex must activate all \(n\) independent inequalities \(\sum_{j\ne q}r_j\le1\). Any at most \(m\) nonzero vertices share a facet. A norm-one functional on the finite absolute \(c_0\)-sum has a maximizing positive vertex; normalized coordinate slices then lift into the given slice. \(\mathrm{P3}\) for \(c_0\) supplies norm-one coordinate averages and the common facet makes the assembled average have norm one. Conversely, \(m+1\) coordinate slices force each off-target coordinate below \(\alpha\), and their equal average has norm at most \(m(1+m\alpha)/(m+1)<1\) for \(\alpha<m^{-2}\). This proves both sides for every integer \(m\ge2\) without finite sampling.

value.rationale: The focal paper asks whether finite convex-combination properties are determined by low arity and proves a complete binary collapse for \(\mathrm{P1}\) while only separating the binary and unrestricted versions of \(\mathrm{P3}\). Showing \(\mathrm{P3}^{(m)}\) but not \(\mathrm{P3}^{(m+1)}\) for every \(m\) gives the natural complete opposite picture for \(\mathrm{P3}\): there is no finite collapse at all. The proof provides a uniform geometric mechanism through common facets of an explicit family of absolute norms, so this is a structural hierarchy theorem rather than a routine parameter increment.
